chapter_theme: Dread of begging: never asking, even from the best givers, is worth ten million times what asking could bring. The chapter's fury goes so far as a curse on whoever ordered the world so that begging is needed, and it holds the withholder guiltier still.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the cruelty of begging (1061-1062), it is no way out of poverty (1063), the worthy don't do it (1064), what one's own effort yields (1065), not even for virtue's sake (1066), begging at the cost of honour is forbidden (1067), and the faults of asking and refusing together (1068-1070).

1061.reading: Not asking, even from those precious as eyes who give gladly without concealing, is worth ten million times more.
1061.nuance: The verse picks the best case for asking, then refuses it. Parimelazhagar narrows this: it's about not asking even friends who already know of one's poverty, and he concludes one should try to live by hard effort.

1062.reading: If even by begging one must live, let the one who made the world wander and perish.
1062.nuance: The Kural's sharpest line against any cosmic order. It doesn't assert that a creator exists, since the curse is conditional. Kalaignar makes that explicit: the one 'said to be' the creator.

positions.position: The creator decrees each being's livelihood along with its karma at conception; if that includes begging, the evil returns on him and he should suffer the same.
positions.quote: சில உயிர்க்கு இரத்தலையும் ஒரு செய் தொழிலாகக் கற்பித்தானாயின், அத்தீவினையால் தானும் அத்துன்பமுறல் வேண்டும்

positions.position: The verse is about those who choose to beg to survive; the conclusion is that death is better than begging.
positions.quote: இஃது இரக்கு மதனின், இறத்தல் அமையு மென்றது.

positions.position: He distances himself from the idea: it is whoever is 'said' to have created the world.

1063.reading: Nothing is harder than the hardness that says 'we will end the misery of poverty by begging'.
1063.nuance: வன்மை, hardness, is the opposite of what one would expect of an asker's position. Begging isn't weakness here but a kind of obstinate insensitivity. Manakkudavar adds that it doesn't even work, since it won't end poverty.

1064.reading: The worth that won't consent to asking even when no means remain is too great for all of space to contain.
1064.nuance: இடம் is used twice: as all of space, and as means or room. A man with no room left holds something that no room can hold.

1065.reading: Though it is gruel thin as clear water, nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort brought.
1065.nuance: தாள், literally the foot, stands for effort. Sweetness has become a moral quality here and doesn't describe the taste. Parimelazhagar says it's equal to ambrosia, because it's one's own.

1066.reading: Even if one asks for water for a cow, nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking.
1066.nuance: A limit case with the worthiest cause and the smallest request, and it's still degrading. Parimelazhagar: virtue itself should be done by effort, never by begging. He also notes that நாவிற்கு confines the disgrace to the spoken word, and that this still exceeds every other disgrace.

1067.reading: I beg of all who beg: if you must beg, don't beg of those who conceal.
1067.nuance: The poet himself takes on the posture he has just condemned, begging beggars. The repetition of இரப்பன், இரப்பாரை and இரப்பின் is almost a chant.

1068.reading: The unsafe boat called asking will split apart when it strikes the rock called concealment.
1068.nuance: The sea of poverty is supplied by both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar. The verse's point isn't the rock alone: the boat itself is flawed, and this is what ஏமாப்பில் says.

1069.reading: Thinking of begging, the heart melts; thinking of concealment, even what remains is gone.
1069.nuance: The heart has two stages: it melts, and then there's nothing left to melt. Concealment is ranked as the worse.

positions.position: The melting heart is that of an onlooker who imagines the cruelty; he notes that all others say it's the asker's.
positions.quote: இதற்குப் பிறரெல்லாம் 'இரக்கின்றவர் உள்ளம் உருகும்' என்று உரைத்தார்.

positions.position: It concerns the asker, who has nothing to gain.

1070.reading: As the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal, where does the life of the one who conceals hide?
1070.nuance: The rhetorical question is a charge: the word that kills the hearer ought to kill the speaker first. Parimelazhagar glosses 'life goes' as being stunned with helplessness, a less literal sense than the verse's own. He reports another reading as a dread-filled man's speech.

links.note: 377 says that even those with crores enjoy only as the apportioner apportioned. 1062 curses that very apportioner, if the portion includes begging. The chapter on fate accepts the apportioning, and this chapter refuses it, and Parimelazhagar's gloss makes the two nearly the same figure.

Gruel is sweeter than ambrosia twice. 64: when one's child's little hand has stirred it. 1065, in Parimelazhagar's reading: when one's own effort earned it. The two supply the Kural's two sources of value in a poor meal, love and independence.

A flimsy vessel breaks up in both. 1134's raft of shame and good manliness is swept away by the flood of love. 1068's boat of asking is split by the rock of concealment. Each shows a failed crossing, but the vessel in 1134 is what one is proud of.
971 calls one's radiance the wealth of aspiration, and 1064 gives its most extreme form. Without means to live, the refusal itself is too large for the world.

source_issues: 1061: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and ends with இது பரிமேலழகருரை, so it is Parimelazhagar's commentary, not Manakkudavar's.
1065, 1067, 1070: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
1063: Pope's gloss turns வன்மை, hardness, into 'folly', and adds 'rather than by working' from the commentary.
1070: Pope's couplet says 'the shamefaced asker dies' while the verse says only உயிர் போஒம்; his gloss adds that the word would kill the refuser, which is drawn from commentary.
